title: Buckingham $\pi$-Invariant Test‑Time Projection for Robust PDE Surrogate Modeling
claim: Inputs and outputs span widely varying length scales, and normalized dimensionless fields lose information where inputs vanish.
layout: 3x4 grid of heatmaps, rows by case, black arrows marking information loss
description: A grid of jet-colormap heatmaps with three rows and four columns. Rows are labeled on the left: Thermal (Length Scale: 1), Thermal (Length Scale: 100) and Stress (Length Scale: 10). The first row's columns are headed k, q, T and π_th. The third row's columns are headed E, f, σ and π_el. The second thermal row has no separate headers. Inputs (k, q, E, f) lead to output fields (T, σ). The fourth column shows the pixel-wise π fields on white backgrounds. These are blank wherever q or f is near zero. Black arrows point at the π panels, and a vertical label on the right reads 'π-Information loss (Degeneracy)'. The eye goes first to the saturated blue-red maps, then to the sparse π panels and the arrows.
caption: The PDE datasets for thermal and linear elasticity. With given distributions of k, q, E, f, the surrogate model predicts the fields of T and σ in each case (Thermal and Stress). Pixel-wise π values go to zero when q →0 and f →0, which is described as π-information loss.
abstract: PDE surrogate models such as FNO and PINN struggle to predict solutions across inputs with diverse physical units and scales, limiting their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. We propose a $\pi$-invariant test-time projection that aligns test inputs with the training distribution by solving a log-space least squares problem that preserves Buckingham $\pi$-invariants. For PDEs with multidimensional spatial fields, we use geometric representative $\pi$-values to compute distances and project inputs, overcoming degeneracy and singular points that limit prior $\pi$-methods. To accelerate projection, we cluster the training set into K clusters, reducing the complexity from O(MN) to O(KN) for the M training and N test samples. Across wide input scale ranges, tests on 2D thermal conduction and linear elasticity achieve an average MAE reduction up to $\approx 91\\%$ with minimal overhead. This training-free, model-agnostic method is expected to apply to more diverse PDE-based simulations.
